paper_title: LLM-Attack Suite: A Unified Red-Team Framework for Privacy Evaluation of Split and Distributed LLM Systems

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Split language models keep input text on a client but send intermediate representations to a server. Attacks can reconstruct text from these messages. Comparing privacy evaluations is difficult when attackers see different messages, know different model weights or use different datasets and recovery measures. We present LLM-Attack Suite, a framework that records these choices and lets researchers check, compare and extend an evaluation. Compatible attacks reuse recorded messages, and their predictions are saved for independent scoring. The scoring rule requires a linked undefended reference before a defence can pass. Reports also identify attacks that remain untested. In a controlled GPT-2 experiment, adding gradients returned during training increased token recovery from 94.20% to 97.38% and exact-document recovery from 13.71% to 37.77%. The 95% interval for the token gain lay above the two-percentage-point threshold fixed before testing. This experiment is shared with a companion study; here it tests how the evaluation responds to a change in attacker access. Further studies measure how corpus choice and compression defences affect recovery, compare an adapted published attack with its reference implementation, and test the measurement code. The framework reports implementation checks separately from measured attack effectiveness. Each privacy claim should state the attacker, dataset and scoring rule, report its controls and identify untested attacks.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Split learning divides language model between client and server [19]. The client keeps the input text and runs the first layers. It sends the server an activation, the intermediate representation computed at each token position. During training, the server returns gradient, which describes how changes to these representations would affect the training loss. Both messages contain information about the private text. Prior attacks reconstruct text from gradients [22, 3, 1], activations [12, 14] or both [2]. Their results depend on which messages the attacker sees, which model weights it knows and how much public text and computation it uses. The dataset and recovery measure also matter. defence can appear effective when the attack already fails without it. An average token score can conceal exact recovery of complete documents or sensitive spans. Researchers need these details to interpret privacy result and compare it with another study. What must an evaluation record and test so that another researcher can check its conclusion, compare it fairly and extend it? LLM-Attack Suite1 records what the attacker can observe, what it knows and the resources it uses. Compatible attacks run on the same recorded messages. The framework requires linked undefended reference before candidate defence can pass its scoring rule, and reports missing tests explicitly. Saved predictions let other researchers check the scores without rerunning the target model. The suite also includes attacks on serving, applications and agents; this paper evaluates privacy in split and distributed systems. 1The suite was previously called LLM-Attacker. Existing software identifiers and frozen evidence may retain the earlier name for reproducibility. The separate autonomous-driving framework of Mei et al. [10] is discussed in Section 7. 1 The experiments test why these choices matter. Matched reconstruction comparisons measure the effect of adding gradients to the attackers observations. Separate studies vary the dataset and defence. Comparisons with published attack implementation check agreement on specified inputs, while tests of the measurement code check scoring, controls and handling of the saved evidence. These checks establish different properties and are reported separately. The contribution has three parts: common evaluation procedure. We specify how to record the model, attacker access, data and resources, and how compatible attacks reuse the same observations. Checkable privacy results. We combine dataset-specific baselines, linked undefended controls and reports of missing tests, and retain predictions and configurations for independent scoring. Evidence for the procedure. We assess controlled reconstruction, agreement with published implementation and the measurement code. The registry records the available validation evidence for all 64 modules, including three orchestration helpers. This methodological contribution builds on two related studies. Politis and Pappas [16] audit real two-node split-training system whose forward-message privacy check missed leakage through the returned gradient. Their study diagnoses that systems failure and tests observation coverage and probe calibration. companion study by the same authors [17] examines how attacker observations and model knowledge affect per-token and per-document leakage. The controlled GPT-2 experiment reported here is shared with that study and provides one evidence base. Here we use it to assess the evaluation procedure alongside additional corpus, trainingduration, defence and implementation studies. The broader Qwen and Mistral experiments provide further system and implementation checks under their own stated conditions.

sections.title: 2.1 Threat model
sections.content: The principal attacker passively observes the messages crossing one split. It sees activations during training and inference, and returned gradients during training. It neither modifies the traffic nor receives the private text, next-token labels or server layers. The capture harness computes the loss using the labels but does not expose them to the predictor. The scorer uses the text afterwards. This observation contract differs from an active server that controls returned tensors, and from server that directly holds the loss labels. By default, the attacker holds public copy of the clients layers, the pretrained layers available for download. stronger condition supplies the trained copy, including the clients fine-tuned embeddings. The attacker also receives public calibration text. Labelled-example, key-solving, active-server and side-channel modules declare their additional privileges separately. Supplementary Section S1 maps the observation surfaces and their associated modules.

sections.title: 2.2 A worked comparison
sections.content: Consider the experiment at split after GPT-2s sixth layer, with the attacker holding public client layers. We want to measure what returned gradients add to reconstruction. The model checkpoint, held-out documents and public calibration text used to fit the attacker stay fixed. 1. Record the observations. Run the target on the evaluation documents and save its activations and returned gradients. Give the activation-only attacker the activations. Give the joint attacker both messages. Neither attacker receives the evaluation text or next-token labels. 2 2. Match the reconstruction search. Both attacks consider 32 candidate tokens per position and keep two partial reconstructions at each search step. The joint attacker uses gradients to propose some candidates. Shuffled-gradient and random-candidate controls test whether any gain depends on the gradient information. Matching the search does not match total computation; the joint attacker also ranks candidates using gradients. 3. Score the saved predictions. separate scorer compares predictions with the held-out text. Token recovery rises from 94.20% to 97.38%; exact-document recovery rises from 13.71% to 37.77%. Exact-document recovery requires every token in document to be correct. Save the predictions and settings so another researcher can check both measures. This comparison isolates change in attacker observations while fixing the stated search limits. It also shows why the recovery measure must be reported: the gain in complete documents is much larger than the token gain suggests. The statistical analysis and detailed attack mechanics appear in Sections 4.1 and 5.1.

sections.title: 2.4 Modules, coverage and evidence
sections.content: Each module declares its supported modes, input requirements, threat metadata and execution function. The registry rejects duplicate names. run writes configuration, threat model, provenance and results to common record, retaining completed measurements if execution stops. new attack can therefore enter frozen comparison through the same input and output contract, with its own controls and budget. Three outputs answer different scientific questions. The scorecard evaluates the measured outcomes under the declared rule. The coverage report marks applicable threats as covered, partial, unmeasured or out of scope. The module-validation matrix records each implementations qualification status as reference conformance, adaptation, real-model qualification, synthetic qualification or unmeasured capability. An execution failure is not negative attack result, and registration alone is not real-model validation. The complete matrix is Supplementary Table S15. The evidence procedure checks files against retained hashes, recomputes metrics from predictions and regenerates predictions from pinned inputs. Optional hash-chained journals reveal edits, deletion or reordering relative to retained hashes. An unsigned chain can be recomputed, so it does not authenticate an untrusted producer. Scientific validity instead rests on the protocol, controls and reproducible analysis. Changes to the attack set or scoring policy receive new versions, preserving earlier results for comparison. These operations serve three research tasks. Attack developers compare new module on existing captures. Defence researchers vary the target while holding the evaluation plan fixed and measure both leakage and utility. Reviewers verify and re-score the retained evidence before attempting full regeneration.

sections.title: 4.1 Controlled reconstruction
sections.content: The principal experiment uses GPT-2 124M [18], split after layer three or six, and pinned 32-token WikiText-2 passages [11]. Each run uses 32 public calibration, 128 training and 256 held-out evaluation documents. Ten independently seeded models are fine-tuned with AdamW [9], then frozen and attacked with two attack seeds. The fixed snapshot supplies activations from the client layers and gradients of the next-token loss averaged over all 256 evaluation documents. The public and trained layer conditions are evaluated separately. The activation-only attacker fits ridge decoder from public activations to token embeddings, selects 32 candidate tokens per position and uses width-two beam search to match recomputed activations. The joint attacker keeps 16 activation candidates and adds 16 from the negated gradient at the previous position, filling overlaps from the activation list. The first position retains activation candidates. Candidate count and beam width are matched. Shuffling gradients between documents and replacing their candidates with random tokens remove gradient information while preserving the search structure. backward-only heuristic provides gradient-only comparator. Full mechanics appear in Supplementary Section S2. The primary test was fixed in advance. At depth six with public layers, the 95% interval for the joint-minus-activation token gain must lie above two percentage points. The bootstrap resamples trained models and documents independently, using 100,000 replicates and seed 93281. Fortyseven secondary contrasts use Bonferroni-corrected bootstrap intervals. The campaign contains 3,200 training measurements and 480 explicitly reused activation-only inference measurements, giving 3,680 records over the same held-out set. All records and journals re-verify against their manifests.

sections.title: 5.1 Returned gradients increase reconstruction
sections.content: The primary test passed. At depth six with public client layers, the joint attack recovered 97.38% of tokens against 94.20% for activation-only reconstruction, gain of 3.17 percentage points, with 95% interval [2.72, 3.64]. Exact-document recovery rose from 13.71% to 37.77%  (Table 1)  . All 47 secondary contrasts favoured the joint attack after Bonferroni correction. The shuffled-gradient and random-candidate controls recovered 93.91% and 93.89%, respectively, compared with 49.98% for the backward-only heuristic. The joint gain therefore depends on the gradients information, not simply on replacing half the candidates. Gaussian gradient noise at 0.1 times the per-document root mean square and eight-bit quantisation left recovery at 97.31% and 97.33%. Figure 2 shows the wider range across attack configurations. At the same undefended depth-six boundary, exact-document recovery varies from 1.70% to 58.55%. These configurations differ in observation, knowledge and effort. Table 1 supplies the matched comparison. Defended comparisons also separate token, document and utility outcomes. Secret mixup, which blends each activation with private decoy from an earlier batch, left 83.0190.67% token recovery while limiting exact-document recovery to at most 1.48%. Name-span recovery remained 47.8566.15% across 716 annotated spans in 249 documents. The annotations were fixed before the run, with AI assistance for names; these are semantic annotations, not human gold labels. Geometric-mean perplexity rose by 31.8% at depth three and 26.9% at depth six. Replica median, an integrity defence that sends activations unchanged, kept token recovery within two-thirds of point of its undefended comparator. Supplementary Section S3.1 gives the defended protocols and full span results.

sections.title: 5.3 Published-attack conformance and comparison
sections.content: Our BiSR port and the archived reference produced identical tokens in all 3,072 paired predictions under the single-seam contract. This establishes implementation conformance on those inputs before comparison with other attacks. In the adapted experiment, refined BiSR recovered 93.21% at depth six with public layers, against 97.38% for the joint attack. The paired difference was 4.17 percentage points, with 95% interval [4.79, 3.53]. With trained layers, the difference was 0.02 points, interval [0.63, 0.58]. Across 15 prespecified secondary contrasts, ten intervals lay below zero, one above and four crossed zero. The configurations in Table 3 show why the framework retains several attacks and their budgets rather than naming universal winner.

sections.title: 5.4 Validation of the measurement procedures
sections.content: We selected 25 existing development-test functions before rerunning them from the reviewed framework revision. Parameterisation yielded 37 cases covering recovery metrics, score calculations, control eligibility, observation boundaries, solver fidelity, resampling and evidence validation. The design combines known-answer fixtures, independent calculations, fault injection and metamorphic tests of prescribed relationships between outputs under controlled changes to inputs [20]. Inputs comprised constructed sequences and arrays, small randomly initialised models and synthetic evidence records. All 37 selected cases matched their expected outcomes, with no failures or skips. Changing text available only to the BiSR scorer left predictions byte-identical. Supplying that text to the predictor was rejected. Removing or weakening required positive control prevented candidate pass. In dependence stress case, increasing perfectly correlated document columns from two to 500 preserved the interval [0, 1] instead of treating copies as independent evidence. Intact evidence was accepted and the specified corruptions rejected. These fixed-case results establish conformance of the selected measurement procedures, complementing reference conformance and real-model experiments. Supplementary Table S11 reports all seven property groups and their case counts.

sections.title: 6 Cumulative Evidence and Scope
sections.content: Taken together, the programme establishes consequential leakage under several independent protocols. The findings include exact structural leakage in deployed Qwen split-training system, high text reconstruction in the controlled GPT-2 campaign, and further corpus-, placement-, depthand defence-dependent failures. The Qwen audit recovered the real/decoy partition on all 8 4,096 frames in its main run even though the forward-only privacy gate passed [16]. Structural recovery and text reconstruction remain distinct outcomes. The broader qualification programme covers Qwen3-0.6B, Qwen3-8B, Qwen3.5-27B, Qwen3.535B-A3B, Mistral-7B-Instruct and Mistral-NeMo-12B-Instruct in diagnostic, ablation, robustness, obfuscation and agentic roles. These campaigns record expected, negative and privacy-breaking outcomes across multiple models and defences. They establish that modules have been exercised under their declared contracts, alongside the controlled GPT-2 recovery results. Supplementary Table S10 records each protocols threat model, module, control, model, corpus, budget, outcome, comparator and evidence tier. The live agentic tier illustrates the importance of retaining negative outcomes. Qwen3-0.6B planner with reasoning disabled produced measurable actions in all ten fixed settings and no policy violation in twenty trials, but blocked all six sanctioned peer-request trials. This qualifies planner/tool integration and identifies over-blocking. It does not establish general agentic security. Synthetic qualification, reference conformance and target-specific security measurements occupy separate tiers throughout the module matrix. The strongest quantitative reconstruction comparisons in this paper concern GPT-2 124M under the stated corpora, lengths and budgets. Their main value for the framework is that changing protocol component changes the conclusion, while retained captures and predictions make that change inspectable. Corpus-specific baselines, utility measurements and matched controls supply the interpretation. Aggregating different protocols into single success rate would discard it. Longer contexts, new targets and additional attack budgets can extend the evidence through the same procedure. All experiments used author-controlled systems. Live endpoint modes require an explicitly supplied host, and the agentic planner accepts local model targets only.

sections.title: 7 Related Work
sections.content: VFLAIR-LLM [7] combines configurable split inference and fine-tuning with attacks and defences. garak [4] organises security probing through generators, probes, detectors and reports, while ML Privacy Meter [13] measures training-data privacy risk through membership inference. LLMAttack Suite concentrates on the experimental contract for split and distributed systems, covering explicit observations and knowledge, shared captures, linked controls, execution coverage and versioned evidence. Our comparisons test the consequences of those choices. Mei et al. [10] introduced LLM-Attacker for LLM-guided closed-loop adversarial scenario generation in autonomous driving. Our suite was previously released under the same name. LLM-Attack Suite provides modular attacks against LLM systems, with this paper focusing on split and distributed privacy evaluation. Gradient reconstruction includes DLG [22], TAG [3] and LAMP [1], while activation inversion includes Vec2Text [12] and SipIt [14]. BiSR [2] combines learned inverter with gradient and activation refinement for split fine-tuning. We assess its reference conformance under the local single-seam contract and compare the adaptation with fixed-budget alternatives. The remaining modules are local implementations or adaptations with their evidence tiers stated separately, not claims of reproducing every cited papers complete protocol. Earlier split-learning attacks demonstrated inversion, model stealing and label inference [15, 6]. Subsequent work examines why depth alone does not guarantee privacy [5] and recovery during split inference [8]. These motivate evaluation across split depths and observation surfaces. The supplementary catalogue records the contracts and qualification evidence for membership, side-channel, application and agentic modules. Their endpoints remain separate from the text-reconstruction gate.

sections.title: 8 Conclusion
sections.content: LLM-Attack Suite makes privacy evaluation an explicit, reusable experiment. Its modules share observation contracts and evidence records, its scoring requires baselines and positive controls, and its coverage report keeps untested threats visible. The experiments establish that attacker knowledge, returned gradients, corpus, defence and attack configuration materially change recovery. Reference conformance and selected measurement-validation tests support the procedures used to measure those effects. Researchers can use the same framework to add attacks to retained captures, compare defence revisions and give reviewers predictions they can re-score. Every privacy claim for split model should therefore name its attacker, corpus and scoring rule, report the supporting controls and leave untested attacks labelled as untested.

S1 Threat Model and Setup Figure S1 shows the two parties, the traffic between them and where our attacker sits. The client owns the text and runs the first layers, from the token and position embeddings through the block at the split depth. The server runs the rest: the remaining blocks, the final layer norm and the output projection to vocabulary logits. In training and in inference the client sends the server an activation for each token; during training it also receives back gradient for each activation, which is the next-token loss differentiated with respect to that activation. Figure S1: The client keeps the text and its first layers; the attacker reads what crosses the split. Marker is our attacker, passive observer of the split traffic. Marker is the active server, stronger attacker used only by the active-attack modules. Our attacker watches this traffic at the split and alters none of it. It can be an eavesdropper on the link or an operator of the server who sees only the tensors that cross the split. It records every activation and, in training, every gradient, and it keeps its own copy of the clients layers along with handful of public documents for calibration. The private text and the servers layers stay out of its reach, and so do the next-token labels, which are the text shifted by one position. For this reason we do not treat the whole server as our attacker, since server that computed the loss itself would hold those labels. The code that captures the traffic in our experiments runs the servers layers and computes the loss from the labels, yet it passes neither to the attack; we use the text only to score the attacks. server that alters the tensors or updates it returns, to make the client leak more, is separate and stronger attacker, the active server; only the active-attack modules take that role. The attackers copy of the clients layers is by default the public copy, the pretrained models first layers as publicly released, which anyone can download. As stronger condition we give it instead the trained copy, the clients first layers after training together with the clients fine-tuned token embeddings. The client does not publish these weights; we give them to the attacker to 11 measure what leak of them would add, and we count the time to export them in the attacks cost. Some modules assume stronger attacker still, and each module states which one it assumes. labelled attacker also holds activations whose tokens it knows, either because it chose that text itself or because some source reveals the true token behind an observed activation; we call such source an oracle. label-free attacker has only public text and public weights. Some defences also multiply every activation by secret key and replace the key at each epoch, one full pass over the training data; we call this secret rotation. per-epoch attacker must start again after each new key, while cross-epoch attacker carries information from one key to the next, for example structure that all keys share or key material leaked in earlier epochs. The key-solving modules model these attackers; the one experiment in this paper that runs them uses no rotation (Section S3.2). The same modules run from three positions without code changes: installed next to the defence, probing fleet of machines over network connection, or as relay on the client-to-server link. What crosses each observation point of Figure S2 and the modules that exploit it. S2 How the Attacks Work The strongest reconstruction attack rebuilds document in four steps. The activation-only attacker uses steps one, two and four; the joint attacker adds step three. This attack is self-contained routine, distinct from the registered inversion modules own joint variant, which explores candidates differently. The four steps match the numbered badges of Figure S3. 13 Figure S3: The joint attack takes half of its candidate tokens from the gradient and otherwise runs the same steps as the activation-only attack. The numbered badges correspond to the four stages described below. 1. Learn decoder. The attacker sends 32 public documents through its copy of the clients layers and records, for each token, the activation and the token behind it. From these pairs it fits linear map, ridge regression held stable by penalty on its size, that takes an activation back to token embedding, the vector the model gives each word in its vocabulary. 2. Candidates from the activations. At each position, the attacker applies this map to the observed activation and lists the 32 tokens whose embeddings have the highest cosine similarity with the result, meaning they point most nearly in the same direction. 3. Candidates from the gradient (joint attack only). The gradient comes from the next-token loss, whose target at each position is the documents next token, so the gradient at one position carries signal about the token that follows it. The joint attacker keeps the top 16 candidates from the activation and adds the 16 tokens whose embeddings have the highest cosine similarity with the negated gradient at the previous position, filling any overlap from the activation list. No earlier position predicts the first token, so the first position keeps its activation candidates. 4. Beam search. width-two search reads the text left to right, extending its two leading guesses with each candidate, pushing them back through the clients layers, and retaining the two whose recomputed activations lie closest to what crossed the split. The two attackers try equally many partial texts and part ways only on their candidate lists. In the main experiment the attacker reads one fixed snapshot of this traffic rather than live training traffic. We fine-tune the whole model, freeze it, split it, and pass the 256 evaluation documents through it once. The activations come from the frozen client layers, and the gradients from the next-token loss averaged over all 256 documents. The shuffled-gradient control strips the gradient of its information by giving the joint attacker another documents gradient in place of the right one. The random-candidate control retains the activation half of the list and draws the rest uniformly from the vocabulary, so no gradient enters. The backward-only heuristic uses the gradient alone: at each position it picks the token with the highest cosine similarity to the negated gradient at the previous position, with no activations and no beam search. We also run SipIt [14], which rebuilds the input one position at time: for each position it searches for the token whose activation, given the prefix already recovered, matches the observed one, with budget of steps per position. We implemented the published algorithm ourselves; when the budget runs out it returns the best token it has tried, so its guarantee of exact recovery no longer holds. 14 The experiments also use white-box attack, which knows the defence and searches for continuous token embeddings that, after passing through the clients layers and the defence, reproduce the observed message, then reads off the nearest token at each position. The inversion attack, form of vanilla model inversion, fits the same linear map from activations to embeddings as step one, on its own calibration text passed through the public layers, and reads off the nearest token without beam search. BiSR, or bidirectional semi-white-box reconstruction [2], works in two stages: learned inverter first guesses the text from the forward activations, and an optimisation stage then refines the guess. In our port, the inverter (which the code names SIP) is small recurrent network trained on public text passed through the public layers, and the refinement (which the code names bf) first matches the observed gradient and then matches the observed activation. The primary statistical test fixed in advance is the two-point gain test: at depth six with the public copy of the layers, the joint attackers token recovery minus the activation-only attackers must have the lower end of its 95% interval above 15 two percentage points. The interval comes from bootstrap that resamples trained models and documents independently. The protocol also prespecified 47 secondary comparisons, each tested with Bonferroni-corrected bootstrap interval. The clients model is GPT-2 [18] (124M) on pinned 32-token WikiText-2 passages [11], split after the third or the sixth layer, with 32 public calibration, 128 training and 256 evaluation documents. Training uses AdamW [9]. The attacker holds either the public first layers or the clients trained first layers. It attacks the fixed snapshot described in Section S2: in training mode it reads the activation and the gradient, in inference mode the activation alone. S3.8 Validation of the evaluation methodology We tested whether the evaluation code preserves the intended meaning of recovery measurements and rejects specified errors in their supporting evidence. The design combines known-answer fixtures, independent numerical calculations and fault injection with metamorphic tests: checks of prescribed relationships between outputs under controlled changes to the inputs [20]. For example, changing text available only to the scorer must leave the attacks predictions unchanged, while removing required positive control must prevent candidate pass. We fixed selection of 25 existing development-test functions before re-executing them from the reviewed framework revision on CPU, retaining their original assertions and numerical tolerances. Parameterised inputs expanded the selection to 37 cases across seven measurement properties (Table S11). The inputs were constructed token sequences, numerical arrays, small randomly initialised models and synthetic evidence records.
